To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) plants can induce resistance to herbivores by activating the JA pathway, and can induce susceptibility to phytopathogens by activating the SA pathway, 2) induced susceptibility to phytophathogens can be costly, and 3) induced resistance can have negative effects on other natural enemies.
Induced responses are widespread in plants, including species that possess constitutive chemical defences.
induced resistance and induced susceptibility are widespread phenomena, and that induced resistance is likely to be the more common of the two.

the ecology of plant defence and the interactions between herbivorous insects and plant pathogens.
the ecological interactions between specialist herbivores and their host plants, and between these herbivores and the natural enemies of their host plants.
the ecological interactions between specialist natural enemies (herbivores and pathogens) of a plant species.

induced responses do mediate the ecological interactions between the specialist herbivores and the phytophathogens of an alpine species.

the specialist natural enemies of A. alliariae are able to exploit its pyrrolizidine defence system.

The main takeaway from our work is that
plants are not passive victims, but are able to actively defend themselves against attack, and can also take advantage of the natural enemies of their enemies to further enhance defence.
